units.text: Imagine that we walk around the edge of one square, keeping the square on our left. Now add a second square next to it, and walk around that one the same way. On their shared edge, the two walks go in opposite directions. If we add both walks, which edges survive?

The interior seam cancels. Only the outside edge is left. That small cancellation is the visible side of a theorem that connects a change inside a region to an accumulation around its boundary. We will start on a line, build up to surfaces and volumes, and then prove the same pattern in any dimension. Near the end, it will explain why a common kind of heat and fluid simulation loses nothing between its cells, and one of Maxwell's equations.

On a line, a boundary is just a pair of endpoints, with a sign. The boundary of the interval from a to b is b minus a. If we cut the interval in two, the cut point is the positive end of one piece and the negative end of the other. Add the boundaries and that point disappears.

The same cancellation happens with changes of a function. The change across the whole interval is the sum of the changes across its pieces. For a continuously differentiable function, the fundamental theorem of calculus says that adding the derivative over the interval gives the value at b minus the value at a. This is our first Stokes theorem: an integral over an interval equals a signed value on its boundary.

For a region on a plane, the boundary is no longer a pair of points. It is a collection of oriented curves. Give each little tile a counterclockwise boundary. Neighboring tiles traverse their common edge in opposite directions, so the signed contributions from that edge cancel. When we add every tile, the outside edge survives.

What are we adding along those edges? One useful answer is work: along a small step, take the component of a vector field in the direction of that step. Reverse the step and the contribution changes sign. A differential one-form is a general rule for assigning such a signed contribution to a small oriented step. The vector field is a familiar picture; the one-form is the object we integrate.
Here is a one-form simple enough to calculate by hand: omega equals x times d y. Go around the unit square counterclockwise. Which edge contributes anything? Take a moment.

Along the horizontal edges, d y is zero. Along the left edge, x is zero. On the right edge, x is one and y increases by one, so the whole boundary integral is one. The exterior derivative of x d y is d x wedge d y. On the unit square, its integral is the area, also one.
That wedge symbol records oriented area. Reversing the region reverses its induced boundary direction, and both sides change sign. Signs are part of the geometry, not an optional decoration.

Now lift the interior of a disk into a cap, keeping the circular rim fixed. This curved surface sits in three-dimensional space, but it is still two-dimensional: two coordinates locate a point on it. Orient the cap upward. The matching boundary direction is counterclockwise when viewed from above. Your right hand links the two: curl your fingers with the rim and your thumb points along the chosen normal.

Take the vector field whose components are minus y over two, x over two, and zero. Its curl is the constant upward vector. Around the unit circle, the circulation is pi. The upward flux of the curl is also pi, whether we integrate over the flat disk or over this cap. The surfaces share an oriented boundary. We are comparing the flux of the curl, not claiming that every vector field has the same flux through either surface.

Now the object itself is three-dimensional. Its boundary is a two-dimensional surface. Build a solid out of cubes and give each cube outward-facing arrows. On a shared face, the two outward directions oppose each other. Their flux contributions cancel. Only flux through the outside surface remains.

For a concrete example, take the field x, y, z, divided by three. Its divergence is one. The integral of that divergence over a unit ball is the ball's volume, four pi over three. On the unit sphere, the outward component of the field is one third; multiplying by the sphere's area gives the same answer. This is the divergence theorem. It is a volume version of the same boundary relationship, not the same dimensional surface integral we just used for curl.
Here is a trap. Imagine an annulus: a region with a hole in its middle. Its outside edge is a boundary. Is that the whole boundary? Decide which way each edge should be traversed.

The inner edge is a boundary too, with the opposite orientation. Consider the angular one-form, minus y d x plus x d y, divided by x squared plus y squared. On this annulus it is smooth, and its exterior derivative is zero. The outer integral is two pi; the clockwise inner integral is minus two pi. Together they give zero, exactly as the theorem predicts.

If we keep only the counterclockwise loop around the origin, we cannot use a disk containing the origin for this form: the form is undefined there. The missing hypothesis matters. A hole is not a counterexample to Stokes; forgetting a boundary or including a singularity is the mistake.

Before we generalize, look closely at what a form does with one small piece. Take the one-form x d y from the unit square. At each point, it takes a tangent vector, drawn as an arrow attached to that point, and returns the x coordinate times the arrow's vertical component.

At the point two, one, attach an arrow pointing one unit right and one half unit up. Its value is two times one half, which is one, evaluated at that fixed point rather than integrated along the arrow. What does the opposite arrow at the same point get? And the arrow twice as long?

The opposite arrow gets minus one, and the doubled arrow gets two. A horizontal arrow gets zero, because its vertical component is zero. Attach the original arrow to a point where x is three, and its value becomes one and a half. So at each point, a one-form is a linear rule on tangent vectors, and the rule can change from point to point.

To integrate a one-form along a curve, cut the curve into small steps, evaluate each step at its midpoint, and add. Walk once around the unit circle with straight steps between equally spaced points. For each straight step, shade the strip between it and the vertical axis. Its signed width is the midpoint x value, and its signed height is the change in y. On the left half, both signs reverse, so the area still counts positively. With four steps, x d y adds up to two.

Eight steps give about two point eight three. Sixteen give three point oh six. Sixty four give three point one four. Each sum is exactly the area of the polygon we walked. As the steps shrink, the sums approach pi, the area of the disk, which is the integral of d x wedge d y.

A two-form takes two steps at once. The basic one, d x wedge d y, returns the signed area of the parallelogram the two steps span. Take the steps two, zero and one, one and a half. Two times one and a half, minus zero times one, gives three, which is the area.
Take the same steps in the other order and the value is minus three. The order of the steps is the orientation.
Now slide the tip of the second step down toward the first. Halfway, the value is one and a half. When the second step lies along the first, the parallelogram is flat and the value is zero.

In three dimensions, d x wedge d z does the same thing with the shadow of the parallelogram on the x z plane. Now try d x wedge d x. Both factors read only the x part of each step, so the shadow lies on a single line and has no area. A wedge with a repeated differential is always zero.

Here is the cancellation behind the general proof, worked once on the unit cube. Take the two-form g d z wedge d x, where g is y squared plus x z. On a face where y is fixed, d z wedge d x measures area, so this form measures flow in the y direction.
Its exterior derivative is d g wedge d z wedge d x, and d g has three parts. They are z d x, two y d y, and x d z. Which parts survive the wedge? Take a moment.

The z d x part repeats d x, and the x d z part repeats d z, so both vanish even though neither coefficient is zero. Only two y d y survives. Moving d x from the back to the front takes two swaps, so the sign stays the same. The exterior derivative is two y d x wedge d y wedge d z.

Now check both sides of the theorem. Inside, two y integrated over the unit cube gives one. On the boundary, d z wedge d x vanishes on every face where x or z is fixed. Only the two faces where y is fixed count.

Where y is one, g is one plus x z, and the flow out is one plus one quarter, or five quarters. Where y is zero, g is x z and the outward direction is reversed, so the flow is minus one quarter. Five quarters minus one quarter is one. The x z part does not change with y, so it cancels between the two faces.

We have integrated values at points, one-forms along curves, and area-type quantities over surfaces. The dimension tells us what kind of object we integrate. At each point, a k-form is an alternating multilinear rule on k tangent directions. In pictures, it assigns an oriented quantity to a tiny k-dimensional piece: scaling a direction scales the result, and swapping two directions reverses its sign. Its exterior derivative is a k-plus-one-form: it measures the boundary accumulation around a tiny piece one dimension higher.

For a compact oriented smooth n-dimensional manifold with boundary, and a smooth form of degree n minus one, generalized Stokes says: integrate the exterior derivative over the manifold, or integrate the original form over its induced boundary. The answers agree. We will first prove it for a box, then say exactly what extra tools take us to a curved manifold.

Orient an n-dimensional box using the coordinate order one through n. An n-minus-one-form has one term for each missing coordinate. We can write each coefficient beside the wedge of every coordinate differential except the missing one. Choose an alternating sign for each term. That sign is bookkeeping for the orientation of the corresponding faces.

For example, in three dimensions, minus f two d x wedge d z is the same form as plus f two d z wedge d x. Swap the order and the sign flips. The minus sign is not a new physical effect; it keeps the orientation consistent when we put the directions in our chosen order.

Now take the exterior derivative. For each coefficient, its differential includes a contribution in every coordinate direction. What happens when we wedge one of those differentials with the differentials already in the term?

A wedge product vanishes if the same differential appears twice. Every direction already present disappears. Only the derivative in the missing direction survives. Moving that differential into coordinate order produces exactly the sign that cancels the sign we placed in front of the term.

Add the terms and the exterior derivative is the sum of the partial derivatives, multiplied by the oriented n-dimensional volume form. The resemblance to divergence is deliberate. Now we can prove the boundary identity by applying the one-dimensional theorem, one coordinate at a time.

Fix all coordinates except the i-th. Integrating the derivative in that direction gives the coefficient on the upper face minus the coefficient on the lower face. Now integrate those differences over the remaining coordinates. Fubini's theorem lets us perform the integrations in this order for our smooth functions on a bounded box.

The outward-first convention for boundary orientation gives exactly those two signs. Do this for every coordinate and add the results. Every term of the interior integral becomes the matching pair of boundary faces. We have proved generalized Stokes for an oriented box in any number of dimensions. We used the ordinary fundamental theorem, the wedge signs and Fubini; no picture of a four-dimensional object was needed.

What about a curved manifold? The box proof is the local engine, but there are real steps left. We use orientation-preserving coordinate charts. Interior charts look locally like ordinary space; boundary charts look locally like a half-space. We also use a partition of unity: smooth weights, supported inside the charts, that add to one.

Multiply the form by a chart's weight and work in that chart. On an interior chart, compact support makes the opposite contributions vanish. On a boundary chart, the normal-coordinate calculation leaves the boundary-plane term with the outward-first sign. This is again one-variable calculus inside a higher-dimensional integral.

Apply the local identity to each weighted piece and add. The weights sum to one, so the pieces reassemble the original form on the boundary. Inside, differentiating the weights produces extra terms, but together they contain the derivative of the sum of the weights. That sum is the constant one, whose derivative is zero. The extra terms cancel.

To make that argument rigorous, we use the facts that pullback commutes with the exterior derivative, that integration respects oriented changes of coordinates, and that the required partitions of unity exist. Those are mathematical ingredients, not something the tile picture alone proves. With them, the local calculation gives Stokes on the manifold.

Before the physics, here is an engineering use of the same bookkeeping. Take one square cell, one unit on a side, centered at the origin, and put two fields on it. The first, x over two and y over two, spreads outward. The second, minus y over two and x over two, is the turning field from the cap.

At each edge we can ask two different questions. How much of the field crosses the edge, and how much runs along it? For the spreading field, the outward flux integrated over each edge is one quarter, while the along-edge contributions on its two halves cancel. The net outflow is one, and the circulation is zero.

For the turning field, the crossing contributions on the two halves of each edge cancel. The along-edge integral is one quarter per edge, so the circulation is one and the net outflow is zero. For these fields, net outflow per unit area is the divergence and circulation per unit area is the curl; for a general smooth field, shrink the cell to get their values at a point. Divergence uses the part of the field that crosses an edge, and curl uses the part that runs along it.

Many programs that simulate heat and fluid flow use finite volume methods, which are built on the crossing count. Each cell stores one number, the amount of heat or mass inside it. In each time step, the program computes one flux for each face and moves that amount across it.

Here are four cells holding four, two, one and one. Let the flux across a shared face be one tenth of the difference between its two sides, and close the outer boundary. After one step, what is the total? Take a moment.

Point two moves right between the top cells, point three moves down on the left, and point one moves down on the right. The two bottom cells are equal, so nothing moves between them. The cells now hold three point five, two point one, one point three and one point one. Every flux was added to one cell and subtracted from its neighbor, so the total is still exactly eight.

Now open one outer face and let point two five flow into the top right cell. That cell ends at two point three five, and the total is eight point two five, the old total plus what crossed the outer boundary. The shared faces cancel exactly as the interior seams did in the first picture. So the total is exact up to rounding error, whatever formula computes the fluxes.

That guarantee rests on three assumptions. The cells stay fixed, each shared face gets a single flux used with opposite signs, and nothing is created inside a cell. Conservation comes from that bookkeeping, but accuracy depends on the flux formula and the time step.

A factor of one tenth is safe here. For the standard explicit diffusion update with four nearest neighbors on an equally spaced square grid, stability for every spatial mode requires a factor no greater than one quarter. Faraday's law, next, counts the other way, along edges.

Now for a physical payoff. Hold a wire loop fixed, and let the magnetic field through it change. Faraday's law says that the circulation of the electric field around the loop equals minus the rate of change of magnetic flux through the surface. The minus sign is the direction dictated by the law, not a new sign invented by Stokes.

Stokes replaces the loop circulation with the integral of curl E over the surface. For a fixed surface, the time derivative passes inside the flux integral under the usual smoothness conditions. If the resulting equality holds for every suitable small surface, the local fields satisfy curl E equals minus the time derivative of B. That is the differential Maxwell–Faraday equation. A moving loop needs extra care; this demonstration keeps the loop and surface fixed.

The common pattern is not that the boundary tells us every detail of the interior. Different interior changes can cancel. The theorem says that the particular accumulation described by an exterior derivative is exactly balanced by the original quantity on the oriented boundary, when its hypotheses hold.

Take the boundary of a boundary and the signed corners cancel. The matching operation on forms also squares to zero: take an exterior derivative twice and you get zero. Those facts fit the same structure, but they do not prove Stokes on their own. The theorem is the bridge between integration, the boundary and the exterior derivative.

On a line, that is the fundamental theorem. On a surface, it connects curl to circulation. In a volume, it connects divergence to flux. In any dimension, the proof reduces locally to the same one-dimensional endpoint subtraction, and the charts tell us how to assemble those local facts. Every interior seam has a partner. The boundary is what remains.
